summary: Describes how to compress multiple IP headers, as well as TCP and UDP headers, hop by hop over point-to-point links. Shrinking the headers saves bandwidth, which matters most on slow links.

plainLanguage.summary: Many packets in the same stream repeat the same header information. This RFC describes how a point-to-point link can send that information once and then transmit only the parts that change.

questions: how to compress tcp and udp headers
how does tcp header compression recover from packet loss
what is a context identifier in header compression
how small can a compressed udp header get
subtitle: How point-to-point links can compress IP, TCP and UDP headers while recovering from packet loss.

tldr.problem: On low- and medium-speed links, repeated IP and transport header fields use bandwidth even though many values stay constant across packets in the same stream.
tldr.mechanism: The compressor and decompressor keep a context for each packet stream. A full header sets the context, while later headers send only changing or unpredictable fields.
tldr.outcome: Typical UDP or TCP headers can shrink to 4 to 7 octets including the checksum. Generation numbers, periodic refreshes and TCP repair mechanisms address packet loss.

today: RFC 2507 is a Proposed Standard published in February 1999. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Related specifications include RFC 2508 for RTP header compression and RFC 2509 for use over PPP.

sections.title: Why Compress IP Headers
sections.content:
RFC 2507 specifies per-hop compression of multiple IP headers and TCP or UDP headers over point-to-point links. It covers IPv4, IPv6 base and extension headers, TCP, UDP, and encapsulated IP headers.

Large headers consume significant bandwidth on low- and medium-speed links, especially for small interactive or voice packets. The RFC says typical UDP or TCP headers can be reduced to 4 to 7 octets including the checksum. It also designs the methods to work over links that lose packets.

The method depends on repeated or predictable field values in packets from one stream. A full header establishes the shared state, and compressed headers carry only the information needed to reconstruct later headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Header fields often repeat from one packet to the next. Sending only the changing information can leave more link capacity for the packet data.

sections.title: Contexts and Packet Types
sections.content:
A context is the header state held by both the compressor and decompressor for a packet stream. A Context Identifier (CID) tells the receiver which context to use. CIDs can be 8 or 16 bits for non-TCP streams; TCP and non-TCP streams have separate CID spaces.

A full header carries a CID and establishes or refreshes the context. A compressed header carries the CID and selected changes. The protocol defines FULL_HEADER, COMPRESSED_NON_TCP, COMPRESSED_TCP and COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA packet types. CONTEXT_STATE feedback can identify TCP contexts that have lost synchronization.

Grouping packets into streams is the compressor's choice. The RFC gives optional guidelines for using fields such as addresses, ports and protocol identifiers. Poor grouping reduces compression efficiency but does not cause incorrect decompression.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver keep matching header state for each packet stream. Each compressed header identifies the state to use and supplies the changes needed to rebuild the original header.

sections.title: Keeping Contexts Synchronized
sections.content:
TCP headers use differential coding: changing values are encoded relative to the preceding header. If a packet is lost, later headers may be reconstructed incorrectly. The TCP checksum detects many such errors, and TCP retransmission lets the compressor recognize the loss and send a full header.

For UDP and other non-TCP streams, each context version carries a 6-bit generation value. The compressor increments it when the context changes, and the receiver discards or temporarily stores packets whose generation does not match its context.

Non-TCP compression also uses compression slow-start and periodic refreshes. After a context change, the compressor sends full headers at increasing intervals, up to F_MAX_PERIOD, and sends one after F_MAX_TIME even on a quiet stream. The fixed MIN_WRAP interval is 3 seconds, which limits reuse of a generation value.
sections.plainLanguage: Packet loss can leave the two ends with different header state. Generation values, repeated full headers and TCP retransmission help the receiver recover synchronization.

sections.title: What Compressed Headers Carry
sections.content:
A compressed non-TCP header carries a CID, a 6-bit generation and any fields that change unpredictably. With an 8-bit CID, the smallest such header is 2 octets. A COMPRESSED_TCP header carries the CID, a flag octet, the TCP checksum and only the changed fields required by those flags.

The RFC classifies each header field as NOCHANGE, DELTA, RANDOM or INFERRED. NOCHANGE fields come from the saved context; DELTA fields carry differences; RANDOM fields are sent as-is; and INFERRED fields are reconstructed from the link frame or other fields. A change to a NOCHANGE field requires a full header.

The configured MAX_HEADER limits how much header data is kept as context. Its default is 168 octets. An implementation must not compress only part of a subheader.
sections.plainLanguage: A compressed header identifies its context and includes unpredictable fields or encoded changes. Other fields are copied from the saved context or worked out from the packet length.

sections.title: Recovering from Loss and Reordering
sections.content:
The decompressor can detect many lost TCP headers when the reconstructed TCP checksum fails. The twice algorithm tries applying the current delta again, based on the possibility that a lost segment had the same change. If that fails, a decompressor on a two-way link may send a CONTEXT_STATE packet requesting refreshed headers.

For non-TCP streams, the generation value prevents use of an out-of-date context. Some links reorder packets; a decompressor may retain old and new non-TCP contexts temporarily. For TCP, implementations can use NODELTA headers or add a packet sequence number so the receiver can restore order.

The sequence-number method adds two octets to compressed headers, making them typically 6 to 9 octets. The NODELTA method typically uses 17 octets. A compressor must skip packet sequence number zero, and it must use packet sequence numbers for a stream when its SYN carries the window-scale option.
sections.plainLanguage: When the receiver detects missing or reordered packets, it can request a refreshed header or use sequence numbers to restore order. These recovery methods add some header data but reduce the time spent using incorrect context.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The compression protocol runs over a link-layer protocol and introduces no additional vulnerabilities beyond that link. An attacker who can inject a false full header may disrupt compression, but the RFC notes that the ability to inject arbitrary link-layer packets creates broader security problems.

The RFC advises implementations not to identify packet streams by inspecting encrypted information, even when it is visible to the compressor. Doing so may expose traffic patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Header compression relies on the security of the link that carries it. Implementations should not inspect encrypted fields to group packets because this may reveal traffic patterns.

viz.caption: PACKET TYPES USED BY THE COMPRESSION METHOD

items.title: FULL_HEADER
items.text: Carries a full header and sets or refreshes a context.

items.title: COMPRESSED_NON_TCP
items.text: Carries the context ID, generation and random fields.

items.title: COMPRESSED_TCP
items.text: Carries a context ID and TCP header changes as differences.

items.title: COMPRESSED_TCP_NODELTA
items.text: Carries TCP fields without differential encoding.

items.title: CONTEXT_STATE
items.text: Lets a decompressor report TCP contexts that are out of sync.
